source: Rissland, Ashley & Branting (2006) Case-based reasoning and law, Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3)
finding: AI and law was a main source of case-based reasoning (CBR). The doctrine of stare decisis says similar cases get similar outcomes, but does not say how to measure similarity. Similarity depends on viewpoint and desired outcome.
numbers: Five features that make law a good CBR domain: open-textured concepts, varied tasks (advocacy, adjudication, advising), varied knowledge (cases, statutes), rich linked case repositories, and use of hypotheticals.
limits: Survey, no experiment. Written by the system builders, so it is a self-account.
agent_relevance: Similarity is not fixed. Our analogue-mapping operator must take the goal and side as inputs, not use one global similarity score.
quote: stare decisis mandates that similar cases should be decided similarly.

source: Rissland, Ashley & Branting (2006) Case-based reasoning and law, Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3) - HYPO
finding: HYPO (Ashley 1988/1990, from Rissland and Ashley's 1984-87 work) was the first legal CBR system built on real precedents. It analyses a new case, retrieves cases, sorts them by on-pointness in a claim lattice, picks best cases for each side, writes 3-ply arguments (point, counterpoint, rebuttal), and tests them with hypotheticals.
numbers: Domain: US trade secret law. Key invention: dimensions, fact patterns that move a claim stronger or weaker. Example: Secrets-Voluntarily-Disclosed; more disclosures weakens a misappropriation claim.
limits: Hand-built case base and hand-coded dimensions. No quantitative accuracy test is given in the survey.
agent_relevance: Template for a retrieve-compare-argue loop: retrieve, rank by overlap, argue both sides, then stress-test with edited cases. The hypothetical step maps to our counterfactual and mutation checks (G3).

source: Rissland, Ashley & Branting (2006) Case-based reasoning and law, Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3) - CATO and IBP
finding: CATO (Aleven, Ashley) added a Factor Hierarchy of abstract legal reasons above base factors, so it could explain why a shared factor favours a side and why a distinction matters. Aleven's controlled experiment found CATO taught basic case-based argument skills as well as an experienced human instructor. IBP (Bruninghaus and Ashley 2003) breaks a problem into issues, hypothesises a winner per issue, tests by explaining away counterexamples, and combines issue predictions.
numbers: Aleven 2003 also defined case-selection rules from CATO and HYPO argument criteria and showed value for predicting outcomes. This survey gives no figures.
limits: Teaching result is on a first-year legal writing course; a search summary (not opened) said CATO students were not better prepared for a legal memo assignment.
agent_relevance: Issue-by-issue decomposition with an explain-away test on counterexamples is a concrete, checkable procedure for the map-an-analogue operator.

source: Rissland, Ashley & Branting (2006) Case-based reasoning and law, Knowledge Engineering Review 20(3) - CABARET, GREBE, BankXX
finding: CABARET (Rissland and Skalak 1991) interleaves case-based and rule-based reasoning on an agenda, in US home-office tax deduction law. If all but one rule condition is met (a near miss), cases are used to argue the condition is met or is not necessary. GREBE (Branting 1991) used relational case structure and structure matching, and a heuristic argument-strength score. BankXX (Rissland et al 1996) used best-first search over linked legal sources to collect a balanced set of for and against cases.
numbers: In a blind test a domain expert graded GREBE's analyses and law students' analyses; GREBE compared favourably (no scores given in the survey).
limits: Small expert-graded tests; grades not reported here.
agent_relevance: Legal CBR is rules plus cases, not cases alone: cases patch rule gaps. Fits a schema where cases serve as evidence when a rule check is ambiguous. BankXX's balance rule (stop collecting one side) is a search-stopping heuristic.

source: Rissland, Ashley & Branting (2005) Case-based reasoning and law (earlier draft of the KER survey)
finding: Draft matches the published survey in content. Describes the 'argumentation pyramid': case facts at the base, then dimensions and factors, statutory rules, court-made tests, and finally policies and principles; CBR algorithms navigate among levels.
numbers: Levels: facts, dimensions/factors, rules, tests, policy. SIROCCO turned case knowledge on and off and showed past cases add meaning to general ethics principles.
limits: Same limits as the published survey; not independent evidence.
agent_relevance: The pyramid is a usable memory layout: store cases at fact level but index them by factor and by the rule they bear on.

source: Bench-Capon (1997) Arguing with Cases, JURIX'97
finding: Separates CBR from plain case retrieval. Retrieval finds the closest case and copies its outcome by stare decisis; real legal CBR argues about which similarities and differences matter. Gives an algorithmic account of HYPO and CATO argument generation.
numbers: CATO has 26 trade secret factors. Factors are binary or dimensions (graded, directional). CATO has 8 argument moves (C1 analogise, C2 distinguish, C3 downplay a distinction, C4 emphasise a distinction, C5 and C6 cite a favourable case, C7 cite a more-on-point counterexample, C8 cite an as-on-point counterexample). HYPO uses a 3-ply form: point, response (counterexample or distinction), rebuttal.
limits: A design paper with algorithms; no empirical test. Factors are not raw facts and must be assigned by hand or by rules before reasoning starts.
agent_relevance: Factor assignment is a separate step before reasoning. For an LLM this is the weak link; the later LLM papers test it.

source: Bench-Capon (1997) Arguing with Cases, JURIX'97 - factor hierarchy
finding: In the factor hierarchy, factors are leaves; parents are abstract factors linked positively or negatively. Distinctions can be downplayed or emphasised by routing through abstract factors. Distinguishing can also be done on dimensions: a dimension distinguishes if the cited case was more pro-plaintiff on it than the new case.
numbers: Algorithms named: Dimension Distinction (DD), Dimension Rebuttal (DR), 3-Ply (TP). HYPO could not make two of CATO's moves because it lacked the hierarchy.
limits: Theory only.
agent_relevance: Gives exact procedures that code can run, which fits our rule that the program decides and the model fills slots.

source: Prakken, Wyner, Bench-Capon & Atkinson (2013) A formalisation of argumentation schemes for case-based reasoning in ASPIC+, Utrecht TR UU-CS-2013-002
finding: Recasts CATO-style reasoning as defeasible argumentation schemes. CS1: if the factors the new case shares with a precedent favouring the plaintiff (set p) are preferred over the shared defendant factors (set d), decide for the plaintiff. CS2 argues for that preference from the precedent's outcome. CS3 and CS4 handle distinguishing and substituting factors (a missing precedent factor is cancelled by a defendant factor, or replaced by a similar one).
numbers: Worked example: Mason vs Bryce, common plaintiff factors {F6, F21}, common defendant factor {F1}, outcome Plaintiff. Uses a 26-factor CATO base.
limits: Formal paper; reasoning is only as good as the factor and case database, which it first assumes correct and relaxes later.
agent_relevance: Each scheme has critical questions, so each step can be attacked. A template for checkable analogy steps: state the shared factors, state the preference, state the precedent outcome, then test the undercutters.

source: Prakken & Sartor (1998) Modelling reasoning with precedents in a formal dialogue game, AI and Law 6
finding: Treats a precedent as a rule set by its decision, which can be broadened or distinguished in a dialogue game (cited in the Bench-Capon and Prakken papers read here).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; claim taken from how the opened papers describe it.
agent_relevance: Case-to-rule conversion: a precedent yields a defeasible rule 'shared pro factors beat shared con factors'.

source: Bench-Capon & Sartor (2003) A model of legal reasoning with cases incorporating theories and values, Artificial Intelligence 150
finding: Cases give rise to preferences among competing values; a new case should be decided to keep a theory of value preferences consistent. A response to the critique that case reasoning must use the purposes behind the law. Summary taken from the opened survey.
numbers: Not given in the opened survey.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Adds a value layer to the factor layer: why a factor matters. Could be a slot in the analogy operator: which value is at stake.

source: Ashley (1990) Modeling Legal Argument: Reasoning with Cases and Hypotheticals, MIT Press
finding: The HYPO book. Cited in all opened papers as the founding source.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Primary source to open in the next pass for exact HYPO behaviour.

source: Allen, Bench-Capon & Staniford (c.2000) A Multi-Agent Legal Argument Generator, Liverpool LIAL
finding: Implements HYPO-style argument generation as cooperating agents. Cases hold factors of three kinds: binary, dimension (with strength and direction), and abstract factors in a hierarchy. When a past and a current case are compared there are four classes of factor (shared and favouring each side, plus unshared on each side).
numbers: Agents work in parallel over classified, sorted cases; no accuracy figures found in the text.
limits: A prototype. Date not shown in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Parallel agents for pro and con sides over a shared case base resemble role-separated passes with code doing the sorting.

source: Zheng, Guha, Anderson, Henderson & Ho (2021) When Does Pretraining Help? CaseHOLD, ICAIL
finding: CaseHOLD is a 53,000+ item multiple-choice task: pick the correct holding (the precedent's governing rule) for a citing passage. It tests 'what does a cited case stand for'. Generic models struggle; law-pretrained models gain.
numbers: BiLSTM F1 = 0.4; BERT F1 = 0.6; Legal-BERT gains 7.2 points in F1 over BERT (12% relative). Law students and lawyers solve it at high accuracy. Gains shrink on easier tasks (Overruling: difference 0.5 to 1.6 points).
limits: Pre-2023 encoder models, not chat LLMs. The human benchmark came from a pilot of the dataset; student accuracy figure not extracted.
agent_relevance: Reading what a precedent holds is itself hard and is the first step of reuse. Do not assume an LLM extracts the holding reliably.

source: Savelka, Ashley, Gray, Westermann & Xu (2023) Can GPT-4 Support Analysis of Textual Data in Tasks Requiring Highly Specialized Domain Expertise?
finding: GPT-4 given annotation guidelines classifies sentences of court opinions by how much they help interpret a statutory concept (4 labels: no, potential, certain, high value). It performed on par with the better law student annotators. Chain-of-thought explanation did not help. Small prompt format changes moved results a lot.
numbers: Original guidelines: F1 = .53 single, .52 batch; with explanations F1 .51 and accuracy .40 (vs .46). Updated guidelines raised single-sentence F1 to .57. The consensus labels came from 11 law students plus 2 legal scholars; students split into groups with agreement above .5 and below .4 (Krippendorff alpha).
limits: Absolute F1 is only .5 to .6; one corpus and one task; GPT-4 of 2023. Brittle to formatting.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-quality labels from an LLM are noisy; explanation (CoT) cost accuracy here, which matches our G1 and G2 stance of using code-checked output instead of self-explanation.

source: Dahl, Magesh, Suzgun & Ho (2024) Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in LLMs, J. Legal Analysis
finding: Models invent case law. Asked a direct, checkable question about a random federal case, they hallucinate 58% (GPT-4) to 88% (Llama 2) of the time. Hallucination rises with task complexity and falls for highly prominent cases. Models also accept false legal premises (contra-factual bias).
numbers: Mean hallucination: GPT-4 0.58, GPT-3.5 0.69, PaLM 2 0.72, Llama 2 0.88. At least 49% even on easy reference-free tasks (factual background, procedural posture). Sharp drop above the 90th percentile of case prominence (PageRank).
limits: 2023 models; US federal cases; tests recall of cases from memory, not retrieval-augmented reuse.
agent_relevance: Memory-recalled precedent cannot be trusted. Any precedent in the agent's memory must be retrieved from a stored real item, never recalled by the model. The model also leans toward the premise stated in the prompt (G5).

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray & Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLM Capabilities in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning (arXiv 2510.08710 v2)
finding: Builds a verifiable CATO-style benchmark with three tasks on case pairs: T1 find distinctions; T2 judge whether each distinction emphasises or downplays (needs the factor hierarchy); T3 find all significant distinctions (integrates T1 and T2). Reasoning LLMs ace T1, drop on T2, and collapse on T3.
numbers: 253 test instances per task. T1: 100% for all models. T2: 64.82% (gemini-flash) to 92.09% (gpt-5). T3: 11.46% (gemini-flash) to 33.99% (qwen3-thinking), most below 25%. Qwen3 thinking vs non-thinking on T2: 78.66% vs 30.04%.
limits: Factor representation is given to the model; factor extraction from text is not tested. Few models.
agent_relevance: Multi-step integration fails even when each sub-step is solved. Argues for code integrating per-factor results rather than the model.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Thinking Longer - effort on wrong answers (arXiv 2510.08710)
finding: Models spend more reasoning tokens on wrong answers than right ones. Reasoning effort does not track accuracy across models.
numbers: gpt-5 averaged 4,456 thinking tokens on incorrect Task 2 answers versus 3,081 on correct ones. Average thinking tokens rise from Task 1 (487) to Task 3 (7,025); qwen3-thinking used the most: 2,011 on Task 1 and 9,596 on Task 3.
limits: Token counts depend on model and settings.
agent_relevance: Long thinking is a failure signal, not proof of rigour. Cap budget per operator call and use a code check (supports G1, G7).

source: Zhang & Ashley (2026) Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs? (arXiv 2610.28799)
finding: All 26 CATO factors can be read out from internal activations of three open models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2 2B) with linear probes; sparse autoencoder features give strong single-feature readouts.
numbers: Best-layer single-feature AUC 0.86 to 1.00 for every factor; median AUC 0.961, 0.972, 0.961 across the three models; 78 layer-feature coordinates. Train 3,932 passages, test 3,961 passages.
limits: Synthetic short passages, one factor at a time; TF-IDF also reaches near-perfect AUC, so wording alone separates them, which weakens the claim of an abstract concept. Real multi-factor cases not tested.
agent_relevance: Factors are a representation LLMs can in principle hold. Supports factor tagging as a sub-task, but gives no end-to-end accuracy.

source: Wang et al. (2026) LePREC: Reasoning as Classification over Structured Factors for Assessing Relevance of Legal Issues (arXiv 2604.19464)
finding: On legal issue relevance, GPT-4o and Claude generate many candidate issues but precision is low. LePREC has the LLM turn case text into question-answer pairs (factors) and fits a sparse linear model on them, which beats the LLM baselines.
numbers: Dataset: 769 Malaysian Contract Act cases, 5,690 extracted issues. GPT-4o precision about 62%; method gives a 30 to 40% improvement over GPT-4o and Claude.
limits: Experts labelled, but one jurisdiction; an LLM also generated the candidates; improvement stated in relative terms.
agent_relevance: Same idea as G5: let the model emit discrete features, let code weigh them. A factor-style intermediate form beat end-to-end judgement.

source: Cao et al. (2026) Adaptive Collaboration of Arena-Based Argumentative LLMs, ACAL (arXiv 2602.18916)
finding: Multi-agent LLMs build arguments in a quantitative bipolar argumentation graph with a clash-resolution step, evaluated on two LegalBench tasks (Learned Hands Courts, Hearsay). It beats single-prompt, CoT, RAG and multi-agent debate baselines.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite on Learned Hands Courts: accuracy 70.8%. Hearsay: highest recall 77.6% and F1 76.7%. Gains over baselines are a few points.
limits: These two tasks are rule-classification, not precedent reasoning; small margins; authors' own system.
agent_relevance: Gains from an explicit argument graph are modest. Not a test of case-based reuse.

source: Guha et al. (2023) LegalBench: a collaboratively built benchmark for measuring legal reasoning in LLMs
finding: A 162-task benchmark grouped by legal reasoning type. Not opened this session (PDF would not parse).
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened; no numbers quoted.
agent_relevance: Source of ready tasks for testing an analogy operator (rule-application tasks).

source: Aleven (2003) Using background knowledge in case-based legal reasoning: a computational model and an intelligent learning environment, Artificial Intelligence 150
finding: CATO evaluation and the prediction algorithms built on CATO and HYPO criteria. Only the survey summary was read; the paper itself was not opened.
numbers: The survey says CATO matched an experienced instructor. Exact test scores not read.
limits: Not opened. Next pass should open for exact scores.
agent_relevance: Evidence that case-based argument skill can be taught and measured; the scoring method may transfer to grading our agent.

source: Bruninghaus & Ashley (2003) Combining case-based and model-based reasoning for predicting the outcome of legal cases (IBP), ICCBR-03
finding: IBP predicts trade secret outcomes by issue, using CATO factors, and explains predictions. The survey cites it without figures; accuracy numbers were not read.
numbers: Not recorded (not opened).
limits: Not opened; no accuracy quoted from memory.
agent_relevance: Open next pass; the main numeric benchmark for symbolic legal CBR prediction.

source: Levi (1949) An Introduction to Legal Reasoning
finding: Classic legal-theory account: law proceeds case to case by example, and the rule is made by how earlier cases are compared.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened; background only.
agent_relevance: Supports treating the stored rule as revisable by new cases (the revise and retain steps).

source: Horty & Bench-Capon (2012) A factor-based definition of precedential constraint, AI and Law 20
finding: Formal model: a precedent constrains a new case if the new case is at least as strong for the precedent's winner on the shared factors. Not opened.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened; description from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: A clean decision test: reuse a precedent's outcome only if the new case is at least as strong; otherwise a distinction exists and the model must argue.
